prompt: I often change an answer at the last second. Can you tell from my history whether this is actually hurting me, and if you do not have enough data yet, how will you measure it?
actualResponse:
No — I can't tell you yet. Both your Reading and Listening histories are empty, so there's no record of any answer-changing behaviour to analyse. I'd be guessing if I said it's helping or hurting.

**On how I'd measure it:**

I can't see your screen or your keystrokes, so this has to be tracked deliberately. Here's the method I'd use:

- During a practice paper, mentally flag every answer you change in the final moments.
- After the paper, tally each change into one of three buckets:
  - **Damaging** — right → wrong
  - **Beneficial** — wrong → right
  - **Neutral** — right → right or wrong → wrong
- Then compute: *beneficial changes minus damaging changes*. That net number is what actually answers your question.
- After 2–3 papers, we also look for a pattern — do you change answers more in Part A short-answer questions, or in B/C? That tells us whether it's a confidence issue or a specific question-type issue.

One caution: I have no approved source telling me how the exam treats changed answers, so I won't make any official claim about it. This is purely self-tracking.

**Next step:** still the 20-minute Reading diagnostic — the first data point: **https://app.oetwithdrhesham.co.uk/reading**

prompt: My exam is tomorrow morning. What should I do tonight and tomorrow before the test? I am tempted to learn a completely new Reading strategy.
actualResponse:
Short answer: **don't learn a new Reading strategy tonight.** Tomorrow is not the time for untested techniques — new methods under exam pressure tend to cost you more than they gain. Use what you already know.

**Tonight (keep it light):**
- One short, easy Reading passage — just to stay in rhythm, not to learn anything new.
- Review your own notes/error list, if you have any. If not, skip this.
- Prep logistics: ID, timing of travel, what you're allowed to bring.
- Sleep. This is the highest-value item on the list.

**Tomorrow before the test:**
- Light warm-up only — one short passage or a few Part B questions.
- Don't cram new material. Don't do a full paper — it'll drain you.
- Arrive early, eat normally.

**What NOT to do tonight:** full timed papers, new strategies, all-night cramming, score-chasing.

- I don't know your exam's start time or location, so those logistics are yours to confirm.
